1	\begin{abstract}
2	LLM-based information extraction systems produce systematic ontology constraint violations during autoregressive generation.
3	On SciERC (7 relation types), 15.37\% of extracted triples violate domain/range type constraints; on DocRED (96 relation types), 18.46\%.
4	Violation rates are governed by \emph{constraint tightness} ($\bar{\tau}$, the fraction of type-pair space ruled out per relation): DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, mean 5.68 valid pairs) and SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, mean 24 valid pairs) exhibit comparable violation rates despite a 14$\times$ difference in ontology size.
5	%
6	We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles IE ontology schemas into two composable decoding constraint layers:
7	(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar CFG) enforcing JSON structural validity and restricting entity-type and relation vocabularies to schema-defined values (ET, RV\,$\to$\,0\%); and
8	(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} (TypeConstraintProcessor) enforcing domain/range constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking.
9	The grammar layer is an enabling prerequisite; the two compose via bitwise AND on token-level masks.
10	%
11	On SciERC, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces domain/range violations by 94\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%) while maintaining extraction F1 ({+}0.13pp, $p{=}0.58$, not significant).
12	On DocRED, violations decrease by 45\% (18.46\%\,$\to$\,10.21\%) with significant gains in relation F1 ({+}0.50pp, $p{<}0.001$) and entity F1 ({+}1.23pp, $p{<}0.001$) for Qwen3-8B; Llama-3.1-8B shows substantial violation reduction (DR$\downarrow$90.2\%) with F1-neutral impact. % exp_ids: phase2_docred_full, llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained
13	Results are validated across two models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and two datasets.
14	Compared with post-hoc filtering, decoding-time enforcement preserves true positives and eliminates entity-type violations that post-hoc methods cannot address.
15	\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
LLM-based information extraction systems produce systematic ontology constraint violations during autoregressive generation.
On SciERC (7 relation types), 15.37\% of extracted triples violate domain/range type constraints; on DocRED (96 relation types), 18.46\%---comparable rates governed by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology scale.
%
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles IE ontology schemas into two composable decoding constraint layers:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar CFG) enforcing JSON structural validity and restricting entity/relation vocabularies to schema-defined values (ET, RV\,$\to$\,0\%); and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} enforcing domain/range constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking.
The grammar layer is an enabling prerequisite; the two compose via bitwise AND on token-level masks.
%
On SciERC, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces domain/range violations by 94\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%) while maintaining extraction F1 ({+}0.13pp, $p{=}0.58$).
On DocRED, violations decrease by 45--90\% depending on the model, with significant F1 gains for Qwen3-8B ({+}0.50pp, $p{<}0.001$) and F1-neutral impact for Llama-3.1-8B (DR$\downarrow$90.2\%).
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
The dual-factor mechanism---tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate---explains cross-dataset and cross-model DR reduction differences.
\end{abstract}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (CF=9.90%), phase2_scierc_grammar_only (CF=0.08%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (CF=2.57%), llama_docred_full_s1 (CF=12.02%)
Cross-field consistency (CF) violations are qualitatively different from DR violations: each triple remains individually type-valid, but the same entity may receive different types across relations.
Ablation cleanly attributes CF to the semantic layer (grammar-only: CF\,=\,0.08\%; full S1: 9.90\% SciERC, 2.57\% DocRED for Qwen3-8B; 12.02\% DocRED for Llama-3.1-8B), arising from per-relation independent enforcement.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_grammar_only, phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
The F1 significance divergence between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$) traces to grammar-layer elimination of OOV relation names: DocRED's baseline RV of 29.66\% (5{,}189 false-positive predictions) vs.\ SciERC's 1.39\%.
% exp_ids: phase0_docred_unconstrained, phase0_scierc_unconstrained

\paragraph{Contributions.}
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
We presented OntoCoDec, a framework compiling IE ontology schemas into token-level decoding constraints.
We conducted the first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE, finding that violation severity is driven by constraint tightness $\bar{\tau}$ rather than ontology scale.
Our two-layer architecture---grammar (RV, ET\,$\to$\,0\%) plus semantic (domain/range enforcement)---achieves 45--99\% DR reduction across two models and two datasets while preserving extraction quality.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
The semantic layer introduces CF violations (up to 12.02\%), a systematic consequence of per-relation independent enforcement that remains an open challenge.
Constrained decoding increases parse failures for some configurations (Llama-3.1-8B DocRED: 9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\% unconstrained).
Results cover two 8B-class models under zero-shot prompting; integration with fine-tuned models has not been explored.

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF violations.
Validation with fine-tuned models, larger scales, and non-English ontologies remains to be explored.

\paragraph{Head type masking.}
At a \textsc{HeadType} position, the processor considers the entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ and the current relation type $r_j$ (if already generated).
If $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only that registered type: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\mathcal{D}[h_j])\}$, ensuring consistency with both the entity list and domain constraints.
Otherwise, if $r_j$ is known, the mask falls back to all domain-valid types: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\tau) : \tau \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)\}$.
If $r_j$ is unavailable, no semantic mask is applied.

\paragraph{Tail type masking.}
At a \textsc{TailType} position, valid tail types are computed from $\operatorname{range}(r_j)$; if $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$, the mask further restricts to the registered type when range-valid.
This implements the core prefix-decidable constraint: once $(h_j, r_j, \tau^h_j)$ are known, valid $\tau^t_j$ values are fully determined by $\operatorname{range}(r_j)$.

\paragraph{Head type masking.}
At a \textsc{HeadType} position, the processor considers the entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ and the current relation type $r_j$ (if already generated).
If $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only that registered type: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\mathcal{D}[h_j])\}$, ensuring consistency with both the entity list and domain constraints.
Otherwise, if $r_j$ is known, the mask falls back to all domain-valid types: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\tau) : \tau \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)\}$.
If $r_j$ is unavailable, no semantic mask is applied.

\paragraph{Tail type masking.}
At a \textsc{TailType} position, the head type $\tau^h_j$ is already determined from the decoded prefix.
The processor computes the set of valid tail types \emph{conditioned on} the head type: $\{\tau^t : (\tau^h_j, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r_j)\}$.
If $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$, the mask further restricts to the registered type when it belongs to this set.
This pair-based check is strictly tighter than an independent range check $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r_j)$, because most relations have non-rectangular type signatures (\S\ref{sec:formulation}).
